title: 10 Questions to Ask a Feedback Analytics Vendor in a Demo
summary: What should you ask a feedback analytics vendor in a demo? Ten questions that make them demonstrate on your own data, and what a weak answer sounds like.
body_markdown:
Vendor demos are built to go well. The dataset is clean, the themes are tidy, the dashboard loads in a second, and the person driving has run this sequence two hundred times. You'll leave impressed. Six weeks later, pointed at your actual feedback, you find out which parts of the demo were the product and which parts were the presenter.


The fix isn't a longer demo. It's a different one. Ask the vendor three things above all else: run this demo on our data, open a theme and show me the raw comments inside it, and tell me which theme moved our score and by how much. Those three separate a working platform from a good presenter faster than anything else, because each one has to be demonstrated rather than described. Thematic publishes the full list below, ordered for a single sixty-minute call, because the questions that expose a weak platform are the same questions Thematic is comfortable being asked.


This is a demo guide, not a[request for proposal (RFP)](https://getthematic.com/insights/customer-feedback-analytics-rfp-requirements) . Requirements go in a document you score later, and a proof of concept runs over weeks on labeled data. The demo is the hour where you find out whether the proof of concept is worth booking.


## The 10 questions at a glance


1. **Will you run this demo on our data?** Tests whether the product works outside a curated dataset.
2. **Show me a theme, then the comments inside it.** Tests traceability from conclusion back to evidence.
3. **What happens when customers start using a new word?** Tests whether the model adapts or needs rebuilding.
4. **Show me every channel in one view, with one set of themes.** Tests real consolidation against a channel-by-channel view.
5. **Which theme moved our score, and by how much?** Tests impact measurement against mention counting.
6. **Fix a theme you got wrong, live, without engineering.** Tests who controls the taxonomy.
7. **Ask it a question in plain English and show me the source.** Tests whether the answer is defensible.
8. **How does this reach the 50 people who will never log in?** Tests distribution beyond the analyst.
9. **What will our security and AI governance review ask you?** Tests procurement readiness.
10. **When do we get our first real answer, and who does the work?** Tests time to value and hidden services cost.


## 1. Will you run this demo on our data, not yours?


Send the vendor a sample before the call: at least 500 open-ended responses across two different sources, unedited, including the messy short ones. Ask them to build the demo on it.


The answer tells you more than the demo does. A vendor who agrees and turns it around in days is confident in the product. A vendor who needs a scoping call, a data science resource, and three weeks is showing you what onboarding will feel like. A vendor who declines has told you the curated dataset is doing work the product can't do.


Thematic's published position is that[accuracy](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-feedback-analytics-accuracy) only means something when it's measured on your own data rather than a vendor sample. Watch for the softer refusal too: agreeing to use your data, then presenting only the three cleanest themes from it.


## 2. Show me a theme, then show me the comments inside it


Pick a theme on screen and ask to see the individual customer comments that produced it. Then ask how many clicks that took.


Two clicks is a reasonable bar. Anything more, or any version where the comments open in a separate export, means that when an executive challenges a number in a board meeting, the analyst can't answer in the room. In Thematic, every theme traces back to the raw comments behind it, and the phrases that assigned each comment to that theme sit alongside it.


The weak answer here sounds reasonable: "the model is 90% accurate, so you can trust the aggregate." Aggregate accuracy doesn't help the person being asked which fourteen customers said the thing.


## 3. What happens when customers start using a word your model has never seen?


Every feedback taxonomy is a snapshot of how customers talked when it was built. Then a product ships, a policy changes, and the vocabulary moves. This is the failure that turns a working platform into a maintenance project.


Ask specifically:[how the themes are built](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-powered-customer-feedback-theme-discovery) , whether a new theme appears on its own, and how long that takes. If the answer involves a services engagement, a model retrain, or a quarterly taxonomy review with the vendor's team, price that in. Thematic discovers themes bottom-up from the feedback itself and adapts as language changes, with no rebuild cycle and no professional-services line item to keep it current.


Good follow-up: ask what happened the last time a customer's vocabulary shifted, and what the vendor had to do about it.


## 4. Show me our surveys, tickets, and reviews in one view, with one set of themes


Most platforms can analyze[several sources](https://getthematic.com/insights/evaluate-multi-channel-integration-feedback-analytics) . Far fewer produce one consistent set of themes across all of them, which is the difference between a unified view and four separate analyses in one interface.


Load two or three real sources during the demo. Ask whether "delivery was late" from a survey and the same complaint from a support ticket land in the same theme, counted once. Then ask what happens to the theme structure when a fifth source is added next year.


Ask about non-English feedback explicitly, because vendors describe it loosely. Thematic analyzes non-English comments by translating them into English first rather than modeling each language natively, which is worth knowing up front if much of your feedback isn't in English. Any vendor claiming native multilingual analysis should demonstrate it on your data, in the original language, during the call.


## 5. Which theme moved our score, and by how much?


Volume is the easiest number to produce and the least useful one. The theme mentioned most often is often not the theme costing you the most.


[Mitre10](https://getthematic.com/insights/humanising-hardware-how-mitre10-made-voice-of-customer-actionable-with-thematic) , a New Zealand retail cooperative running a three-person insights team across 84 stores, found that stock availability was mentioned by only 6% of customers but was costing 0.5 net promoter score (NPS) points across the whole store network. Interface complaints raised by 25% of customers cost less. Fixing the low-volume issue first protected revenue that a mention-count ranking would have walked them straight past.


So ask the vendor to break a score movement into what pushed it up and what pushed it down, quantified per theme. Thematic's score-change analysis does this between any two periods. If the demo can only show which themes are growing in volume, you're buying a mention counter.


## 6. Fix a theme you got wrong, live, without engineering help


Find a miscategorized comment in the demo, and ask the person driving to correct it while you watch.


Three things to note. Whether they can do it at all without a support ticket. Whether the fix is a one-off relabel or a rule that applies going forward. And what happens to last quarter's report once the theme changes, because a taxonomy that silently rewrites history breaks trend reporting and any number already sent to a board.


Thematic's published position is that the taxonomy should belong to your team: editable and governable by the people who own the reporting, not by the vendor. So the answer that should end the conversation is "our data science team handles theme changes." That's a services contract wearing a product's clothes.


## 7. Ask it a question in plain English and show me where the answer came from


Every vendor now has a chat box. The demo question isn't whether it answers, but whether the answer is defensible.


Type a real question about your data during the call. Then ask the platform to show which comments the answer drew on, and ask the vendor what happens when the same question is asked twice. Thematic answers plain-English questions with the supporting comments attached, and connects to AI assistants over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so the same grounded data can be queried from tools your team already uses.


An answer with no visible sources is a summary you can't check. That's fine for exploring and unusable for reporting.


## 8. How does this reach the 50 people who will never log in?


Most feedback platforms are bought by an insights team and judged, a year or two later, on whether anyone else in the business used them.


Ask what a department head receives without logging in, whether it arrives on a schedule, and what it costs per person.[Community Health System](https://getthematic.com/insights/community-health-systems-actionable-insights) is a not-for-profit healthcare network in California's central San Joaquin Valley. Its Organizational Development team delivered 250 department-ready reports from open-ended employee engagement comments in a single three-day sprint. That saved more than 160 hours and over $10,000 per reporting cycle, replacing weeks of manual work in Excel. Leaders below VP level got a standard deliverable for the first time instead of requesting ad hoc analysis.


Ask about seats directly, since[per-viewer pricing](https://getthematic.com/insights/per-seat-licensing-feedback-insights) quietly caps how far insight travels. Thematic does not charge per seat for people who only need to see the results.


## 9. What will our security and AI governance review ask you, and can you answer it today?


This is the question that decides whether the platform arrives this quarter or next year. Generative AI vendors get asked things conventional software vendors do not, and the answers are rarely ready.


The[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/govern/) addresses this directly. Its GOVERN 6.1 guidance asks organizations to establish policies covering transparency into third-party system functions, including knowledge about training data, training and inference algorithms, and assumptions and limitations. Your security team will want that, plus certifications, data residency, and access control. Ask for specifics rather than assurances: which certification, audited by whom, how recently, and what happens to your data at termination.


Thematic holds[SOC 2 Type II](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2/) with annual penetration testing, supports SAML 2.0 single sign-on and automated user provisioning through SCIM, and offers data residency in the United States, the European Union, and Australia and New Zealand. Ask every vendor to name their equivalents in the demo, and ask what hasn't been completed yet.


## 10. When do we get our first real answer, and who does the work?


Close the demo here, because the answer reveals the shape of the contract.


Ask for the date of the first usable theme breakdown on your live data, then ask who produces it: your analyst, the vendor's onboarding team, or a paid implementation partner.[Greyhound](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-reducee-analytics-time-tenfold/) is the bus transportation network operating across the United States, Canada, and Mexico. It reduced analytics time tenfold on the free-text fields of a post-trip survey running 100 to 150 responses a day. Issues now surface within two minutes, where the data used to be three to four weeks old before it reached anyone. Matthew Schoolfield, Manager for Commercial Analytics at Greyhound, described the before state plainly: "Previously, only one person, myself, would manually analyze the feedback. It was about 80% of my job." One large grocery retailer cut time to insight from seven days to five hours.


If the answer is "about eighteen months to full maturity," that's the contract being described, whatever the demo looked like. Thematic's answer is days rather than quarters, on top of the existing CX stack. Whatever the number, get it in writing, and ask what the vendor needs from your team to hit it.


## How to run the hour


Sixty minutes won't cover ten questions properly, so sequence them.


- **If you have twenty minutes,** ask questions 1, 2, and 5. Own data, traceability, and impact rather than volume. These three separate real platforms from good demos faster than anything else here.
- **Bring the people who can block the deal.** Someone from security or procurement in the room for question 9 saves a month later.
- **Give one person the job of writing down every answer that was a promise rather than a demonstration.** Those become your proof of concept success criteria.
- **Phrase every "show me" as an instruction, not a question.** "Can it trace back to comments?" gets a yes. "Open that theme and show me the comments" gets an answer.
- **Book the follow-up before you leave the call,** on your data, with this call's promises written down as tests.


Then run a[structured proof of concept](https://getthematic.com/insights/evaluate-ai-feedback-analytics-poc) . The demo tells you which vendors are worth weeks of your team's time. It isn't the evaluation itself.


## The short version


Ask a feedback analytics vendor to demo on your own feedback, trace any theme back to the raw comments in two clicks, quantify which themes moved your score rather than which were mentioned most, correct a wrong theme live without engineering, and name a date for your first real answer. Thematic is built to be tested this way, which is why Thematic publishes the questions worth asking every vendor, itself included. If you change one thing about your next demo, send your data in advance and see what comes back.
